procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Magistrate at Sagar in Criminal Case No. 44 of 1950
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 12th November, 1952, of the High Court of Judicature at Nagpur in Criminal Revision No. 399 of 1951
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants carried the matter further in revision to the High Court but it was dismissed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by Special Leave granted by the Supreme Court by its Order dated the 30th January, 1953

issue.issue_text: Whether a previous acquittal for an offence under s. 7 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, bars a subsequent trial for distinct offences under ss. 392 and 332 of the Indian Penal Code, under the principle of double jeopardy enshrined in s. 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The appellants were previously prosecuted for an offence under s. 7 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, for illegally exporting goods.
Although initially convicted by a Magistrate, they were acquitted on appeal by the Additional Sessions Judge.
Subsequently, they were tried and convicted for offences under ss. 392 (robbery) and 332 (voluntarily causing hurt to a public servant) of the Indian Penal Code.
These later charges arose from the same incident, specifically from their actions of beating a Head Constable and taking back the goods that he had lawfully seized.
law: The appellants argued that their second trial was barred by the principle of double jeopardy under s. 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which states that a person once acquitted cannot be tried again for the same offence or on the same facts for any other offence.
The Court, however, relied on s. 403(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides an exception to this rule.
Section 403(2) states that a person acquitted of an offence may be tried afterwards for any 'distinct offence' for which a separate charge might have been made against him in the former trial.
application: The Supreme Court found that the appellants were not being tried again for the 'same offence' as contemplated by s. 403(1).

It held that the offence of illegally exporting goods (under s. 7 of the Essential Supplies Act) was a 'distinct offence' from the subsequent acts of robbing a public servant and causing him hurt (under ss. 392 and 332 of the Indian Penal Code).

The Court reasoned that while the legality of the seizure was a factor in the second trial, the core issues to be determined were different: whether the appellants robbed the Head Constable of the seized goods and whether they voluntarily caused him hurt while he was discharging his duty.
Therefore, the Court concluded that s. 403(2) was a 'complete answer' to the appellants' contention, as it explicitly allows for a subsequent trial for a distinct offence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument, holding that the previous acquittal for illegal export under the Essential Supplies Act did not bar the subsequent trial for the distinct offences of robbery and causing hurt to a public servant under the Indian Penal Code. The Court found that the subsequent trial was permissible under the exception provided in s. 403(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

issue.issue_text: Whether the absence of mens rea could be claimed as a defense for the offence under section 392 of the Indian Penal Code, based on the appellants' alleged honest belief that they were not illegally exporting goods.

facts: The appellants claimed they honestly believed they were taking goods to a place called Baraitha, which is within the State of Madhya Pradesh.
The lower courts made a finding of fact that the route the appellants had chosen was not the one that led to Baraitha or any other place within Madhya Pradesh.
The route the appellants were on actually led to the State of Uttar Pradesh.
law: In a Special Leave to Appeal, the Supreme Court does not re-agitate questions of fact and accepts the findings of fact from the lower courts as binding.
application: The Supreme Court accepted the lower courts' finding of fact regarding the route taken by the appellants.
The Court reasoned that this factual finding directly contradicted and 'negatived' the appellants' claim of an honest belief.
The fact that they were on a route leading to Uttar Pradesh, and not their stated in-state destination, disproved their assertion that they lacked the guilty mind (mens rea) for illegal export.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the defense of absence of mens rea because the factual finding that the appellants were on a route leading to Uttar Pradesh directly contradicted their claim that they honestly believed they were traveling to a location within Madhya Pradesh.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is permissible for appellants in a Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136 to re-agitate questions of fact and challenge the findings of fact from the lower courts.

facts: The case reached the Supreme Court as a Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
The appellants sought to challenge the factual findings that had been determined by the lower courts (the Magistrate, the Additional Sessions Judge, and the High Court).
law: The Court established a legal principle regarding its jurisdiction in appeals under Article 136.
application: The Court applied the principle that in a Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136, it is not open for the appellants to re-agitate questions of fact.
Consequently, the Court refused to disturb the findings of fact that were arrived at by the lower courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it is not permissible for appellants in a Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136 to re-agitate questions of fact. The Court held that the findings of fact from the lower courts must be accepted as binding and cannot be challenged at this stage.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a previous acquittal for an offence under s. 7 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, bars a subsequent trial for distinct offences under ss. 392 and 332 of the Indian Penal Code, under the principle of double jeopardy enshrined in s. 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The appellants were previously tried and acquitted for an offence under s. 7 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, for exporting contraband goods.

Under s. 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, having been acquitted, they cannot be tried again for the same offence or on the same facts for any other offence for which a different charge might have been made under s. 236 or for which they might have been convicted under s. 237.
respondent_arguments: The subsequent trial is not for the same offence, but for distinct offences under ss. 332 and 392 of the Indian Penal Code (voluntarily causing hurt to a public servant and robbery).
The case is governed by s. 403(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which allows for a subsequent trial for a distinct offence, not s. 403(1).
Sections 236 and 237 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not applicable to this case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the absence of mens rea could be claimed as a defense for the offence under section 392 of the Indian Penal Code, based on the appellants' alleged honest belief that they were not illegally exporting goods.
appellant_arguments: There was an absence of mens rea, which is a necessary element for an offence under section 392.
The appellants honestly believed they were taking their goods to a place within the State of Madhya Pradesh and were not illegally exporting them.
respondent_arguments: The appellants' claim of an honest belief is false, as evidenced by the facts.
The route the appellants had chosen was not the one leading to a place within Madhya Pradesh, but was a route that led to Uttar Pradesh, proving their intent to illegally export.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it is permissible for appellants in a Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136 to re-agitate questions of fact and challenge the findings of fact from the lower courts.
appellant_arguments: The appellants sought to challenge the lower courts' findings of fact, such as the legality of the seizure and whether the goods were being illegally exported.
respondent_arguments: In a Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136, it is not permissible for the appellants to re-agitate questions of fact.
The findings of fact arrived at by the lower courts are binding and should not be disturbed by the Supreme Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person who has been tried and acquitted of an offence can be subsequently tried for a distinct offence arising from the same facts, as the bar on double jeopardy under section 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not apply when the subsequent charges constitute a distinct offence as contemplated by sub-section (2) of that section.
obiter: In a Special Leave to Appeal under article 136, it is not open to the appellants to re-agitate questions of fact and ask the Court to disturb the findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellants' previous acquittal for the offence of illegally exporting goods under the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, does not bar a subsequent trial and conviction for the distinct offences of robbery and causing hurt to a public servant under the Indian Penal Code, as these are not the same offences and are governed by s. 403(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, not s. 403(1). The subsequent offences required proof of different elements, namely robbing a public servant of lawfully seized goods and voluntarily causing him hurt in the discharge of his duties.
legal_tests_applied: Section 403(1) and 403(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Principle of Double Jeopardy / Autrefois Acquit)
Article 136 of the Constitution (Scope of Special Leave to Appeal)
Sections 236 and 237 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Charges for doubtful or different offences based on the same facts)
why_appellant_lost: The Court held that the rule against re-agitating questions of fact in a Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136 meant the lower courts' findings were binding, which directly undermined the appellants' claim of an honest belief regarding their destination.

The appellants' argument regarding the absence of mens rea was rejected because the binding factual finding from the lower courts established that the route they had chosen was not one that led to a place within Madhya Pradesh, but one that led to Uttar Pradesh, thus negating their claim of an honest mistake.

The double jeopardy claim under s. 403(1) failed because the subsequent trial was not for the same offence. The offences of robbery (s. 392 IPC) and causing hurt to a public servant (s. 332 IPC) are distinct from the offence of illegal exportation under the Essential Supplies Act.

The Court found that neither s. 236 nor s. 237 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applied to the case, which was a necessary condition for the appellants to invoke the broader protection of s. 403(1) regarding different charges on the same facts.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the case was governed by s. 403(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which permits a subsequent trial for a distinct offence, was accepted by the Court as the correct interpretation.

The Court agreed that the offences under ss. 332 and 392 of the Indian Penal Code were distinct from the earlier offence. While the legality of the seizure (related to the export) was a preliminary issue, the core of the new charges involved the separate acts of robbing the Head Constable and causing him hurt.
The respondent's argument that findings of fact from lower courts are not to be disturbed in an appeal under Article 136 was explicitly upheld by the Court.

The factual findings accepted by the Court, specifically that the appellants were on a route to Uttar Pradesh, directly supported the respondent's contention that the claim of an honest belief (and lack of mens rea) was false.
policy_considerations: In a Special Leave to Appeal under article 136, it is not open to the appellants to re-agitate questions of fact and ask the Court to disturb the findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below. Those findings must therefore be accepted as binding.
